blocks.content: The chi-square ($ ^2 $) distribution is a special case of the gamma, as a $ ^2 $ random variable with $ n $ degrees of freedom follows a gamma distribution with parameters $ = n/2 $ and $ = 1/2 $ ($ = 2 $), namely, $ _n^2 (2, 1/2) $, giving the density function as $$ p(x\mid n)=\frac{2^{-n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2)}x^{n/2-1}e^{-x/2} $$ Hence for $ x _ n ^ 2 $, $$ p(x)\propto x^{n/2-1}e^{-x/2} $$

The inverse-gamma distribution will prove useful as a conjugate prior for Gaussian likelihoods with unknown variance. It is defined by the distribution of the random variable $ y = x^ -1 $, where $ x (,) $. The resulting density function is $$ p(x\mid\alpha,\beta)=\frac{\beta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{-(\alpha+1)}e^{-\beta/x}\quad for\alpha,\beta,x>0 $$

The mean and variance for this distribution are only defined (i.e., finite) if $ $ is sufficiently large, with $$ \mu_{x}=\frac{\beta}{\alpha-1}\quad for\alpha>1\quad and\quad\sigma_{x}^{2}=\frac{\beta^{2}}{(\alpha-1)^{2}(\alpha-2)}\quad for\alpha>2 $$
Note for the inverse gamma that $$ p(x\mid\alpha,\beta)\propto x^{-(\alpha+1)}e^{-\beta/x} $$

If $ y _n^2 $, then $ x = 1/y $ follows an inverse chi-square distribution, which is denoted by $ x _n^ -2 $. This is a special case of the inverse gamma, with (as for a normal $ ^2 $) $ = n/2 $, $ = 1/2 $. For $ n > 4 $ (i.e., $ > 2 $), the resulting density function is $$ p(x\mid n)=\frac{2^{-n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2)}x^{-(n/2+1)}e^{-1/(2x)} $$ with a mean and variance of $$ \mu_{x}=\frac{1}{n-2}\qquad and\qquad\sigma_{x}^{2}=\frac{2}{(n-2)^{2}(n-4)} $$

The scaled inverse chi-square distribution is more typically used in a Bayesian analysis, where the rate parameter, $ $ (which equals 1/2 under a chi-square), is replaced by $ = _ 0 ^ 2 /2 $, making the resulting pdf $$ p(x\mid n)\propto x^{-(n/2+1)}e^{-\sigma_{0}^{2}/(2x)} $$ where the $ 1/(2x) $ term in the exponential is replaced by a $ _0^2/(2x) $ term. The scaled inverse chi-square distribution thus involves two parameters $ (_0^2 $ and $ n) $, and is denoted by $ _ (n, _0^2) ^ -2 $ or $ - ^2(n, _0^2) $. Note that if $$ x\sim\chi_{(n,\sigma_{0}^{2})}^{-2},\qquad\mathrm{t h e n}\qquad\sigma_{0}^{2}x\sim\chi_{n}^{-2} $$ which shows that $ _ 0 ^ 2 $ is a scaling factor on a standard $ (= 1/2) $ inverse chi-square.

Gaussian Likelihood With Unknown Variance: Scaled Inverse- $ ^ 2 $ Priors Suppose data are drawn from a normal distribution with a known mean, $ $, but unknown variance, $ ^ 2 $. The resulting likelihood function can be expressed as $$ \ell(\sigma^{2}\mid\mathbf{x},\mu)\propto(\sigma^{2})^{-n/2}\exp\left(-\frac{nS^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right) $$ where $$ S^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-\mu\right)^{2} $$

Notice that since we condition on x and $ $ (i.e., their values are known), $ S^2 $ is a constant. Further observe that, as a function of the unknown variance, $ ^2 $, the likelihood is proportional to a scaled inverse $ ^2 $ distribution (Equation A2.30a). If we take the prior for the unknown variance also as a scaled inverse $ ^2 $ with hyperparameters $ _0 $ and $ _0^2 $, the posterior becomes $$ \begin{align*}p(\sigma^{2}\mid\mathbf{x},\mu)&\propto(\sigma^{2})^{-n/2}\exp\left(-\frac{nS^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)(\sigma^{2})^{-\nu_{0}/2-1}\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)\\&=(\sigma^{2})^{-(n+\nu_{0})/2-1}\exp\left(-\frac{nS^{2}+\sigma_{0}^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)\end{align*} $$

Equation A2.30a shows the resulting posterior is also a scaled inverse $ ^2 $ distribution with parameters $ _n = (n + _0) $ and $ _n^2 = (nS^2 + _0^2) $. Hence, $$ \begin{array}{r l}{\mathrm{t h e~p r i o r~}\sigma^{2}\sim\chi_{\nu_{0},\sigma_{0}^{2}}^{-2}}&{{}\mathrm{y i e l d s~t h e~p o s t e r i o r}\quad\sigma^{2}\mid(\mathbf{x},\mu)\sim\chi_{\nu_{n},\sigma_{n}^{2}}^{-2}}\end{array} $$
